division.heading: Actions Started by Statement of Claim

subdivision.heading: Defence to Statement of Claim, Reply to Defence and Demand for Notice

operative_text.controlling:
3.33(1)  A plaintiff may file a reply to a statement of defence.
(2)  If the plaintiff files a reply, the reply must
(a) be in Form 12, and
(b) comply with the rules about pleadings in Part 13, Division
3.
(3)  The plaintiff must file the reply and serve it on the defendant
within 10 days after service of the statement of defence on the
plaintiff.

BOOK_A.commentary:
Before about 1965, Alberta lawyers used to file replies and joinders which merely denied the last opposing pleading and joined issue;but usually in later years, they have no longer bothered. Alberta Rules generally make it optional whether to reply to the previous pleading of the other party. Only a statement of defence is needed (against a statement of claim, a counterclaim or a

third party notice) to prevent default judgment.Even then, R.13.12 presumes that all the facts in the previous pleading are denied.If one does not file alaterpleading within the time set to do so (such as a reply to a defence), then it is presumed that there is a mere denial and that "issue is joined," i.e., the pleadings are closed.If one may wish to file a Reply or the like, one should get an express agreement (or order) to hold open the time to do so. Where an amended statement

of defence is filed, that re-opens the time to file a Reply. An appeal over amendments to the pleadings does not keep pleadings open. After almost 4 years, the court would not give leave to the plaintiff to file a late Reply, no evidence having been given to explain the delay.

BOOK_B.title: Reply to defence

commentary.text: Rule 3.33 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.33. In Mikisew Cree First Nation v. Canada, 2004 ABCA 279, 2004 CarswellAlta 1188, 354 A.R. 365, 33 Alta. L.R. (4th) 231, the Court discussed what may be included in a reply. At pp. 368-369, the Court said: … Alberta's Rules of Court define a reply at rule 5(1)(o) as “a statement by which the plaintiff answers the defendant's statement of defence” but the Rules do not specify requirements for a reply. However, the reply, like all pleadings, must meet the requirement of rule 110(2) which provides: 110. (2) No pleading shall, except by way of amendment, raise any new ground of claim or contain any allegation of fact inconsistent with the previous pleadings of the party pleading it. Stevenson and Côté in Alberta Civil Procedure Handbook 2004 (Edmonton: Juriliber, 2004) at p. 96, comment that rule 110(2) says that “a reply is not the place to put a cause of action”. Similarly, Goldrein and Jacob in their text, Pleadings: Principles and Practice (London: Sweet and Maxwell, 1990) at p. 161-2, note that a plaintiff must not in a reply make any allegations of fact or raise any new ground of claim inconsistent with the statement of claim. They agree with Stevenson and Côté that a new cause of action is to be pleaded by amending the statement of claim. New causes of action were not permitted in a reply in Udovitch Estate v. Helm Estate (2000), 276 A.R. 147, 2000 ABQB 796, and Kaup v. Weir et al. (1998), 224 A.R. 347 (Q.B.). This requirement does not change because of an amended statement of defence. If the reply raises a new cause of action, then it is an error independent of anything contained in the respondents' pleadings. The Chambers judge was not required to consider the effect of the amended statement of defence when determining whether the reply raised new causes of action. In Laughren v. Rosetown Union Hospital Board (1966), 56 W.W.R. (N.S.) 165 (Sask. Q.B.), relying on Bullen & Leake's Precedents of Pleadings (11th Ed.), at p. 693, four purposes for a reply were listed at p. 170: a) to admit some of the facts alleged in the defence, or to meet them by asserting new and additional facts; b) to plead an objection in point of law; c) to plead in answer to the defence that it mistakes the causes of action; and d) if the defendants has pleaded a counterclaim which the plaintiff desires to contest, to deal with allegations of fact in the counterclaim.
